summary: This informational document proposes an incremental carrier-grade NAT approach for IPv6 transition as IPv4 addresses run out. Host-based methods did not meet every need, so the operator adds NAT in stages. It combines tunneling with NAT.

eli5.summary: With too few old addresses, the internet provider shares them across customers with a big translator, added gradually while moving to the new kind.

questions: how does incremental cgn combine ipv4 nat with ipv6 tunneling
why can the same cgn device support multiple transition phases
subtitle: A gradual approach to IPv6 transition that combines IPv4 address sharing with IPv6 tunneling.

tldr.problem: IPv4 addresses are exhausted, but many ISPs run IPv4-only networks that would be costly and complex to upgrade entirely. Host-based transition mechanisms alone cannot meet all requirements, and ISPs need a way to support IPv6 while keeping their core IPv4 infrastructure largely unchanged.
tldr.mechanism: An incremental CGN approach combines carrier-grade NAT (which shares IPv4 addresses among many customers) with IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling. Dual-stack home gateways tunnel IPv6 traffic over IPv4 to dual-stack CGN devices that forward it to the IPv6 Internet, while simultaneously performing IPv4 address translation for legacy IPv4 traffic.
tldr.outcome: ISPs can support IPv6 for willing customers without immediately replacing their IPv4 networks, and the approach supports smooth evolution toward dual-stack or IPv6-only infrastructure through configuration changes rather than wholesale equipment replacement.

facts.label: Main components
facts.value: Dual-stack home gateway and dual-stack CGN

facts.label: Configuration phases
facts.value: IPv4 NAT only, then 6rd enabled, then native IPv6

today: RFC 6264 is Informational and proposes an approach to IPv6 transition as of 2011. It does not standardize new protocols but recommends combining existing technologies. While IPv6 deployment has progressed significantly since 2011, many ISPs have adopted elements of this hybrid approach. The document remains relevant as a reference for understanding the incremental transition strategies that carriers deployed during the critical years of IPv4 exhaustion.

sections.title: The IPv4 Exhaustion Problem
sections.content:
By 2011, the global exhaustion of IPv4 addresses was imminent. The traditional approach to IPv6 transition assumed that operators would want to deploy dual-stack networks—running both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously throughout their infrastructure. However, many ISPs found dual-stack deployment to be complex and expensive. Some operators instead chose to deploy Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN), which allows them to share a small pool of public IPv4 addresses among many customers. But CGN alone does nothing to transition toward IPv6; it merely delays the transition and perpetuates dependence on IPv4.

The document proposes a different path: incremental CGN, which combines v4-v4 NAT with IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling. This allows ISPs to share IPv4 addresses as a short-term solution while simultaneously offering IPv6 service to customers who need it, without requiring the core ISP network to be upgraded immediately to support IPv6 natively.
sections.eli5: Old addresses are running out. Some providers just add translators; others want to support the new system too. This approach does both at once.

sections.title: The Incremental CGN Architecture
sections.content:
The system consists of two main components. First, a dual-stack home gateway (HG) at the customer premises that handles both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic. For IPv4, it forwards packets to the CGN (optionally performing v4-v4 NAT if the customer has private IPv4 addresses). For IPv6, it encapsulates packets into IPv4 tunnels, using technologies like 6rd (IPv6 Rapid Deployment), and sends them to the CGN.

Second, a dual-stack CGN in the ISP's network receives these packets. When it receives normal IPv4 packets from the HG, it performs standard v4-v4 address translation and forwards them to the IPv4 Internet. When it receives IPv6 packets encapsulated inside IPv4 tunnels, it decapsulates them and forwards them to the IPv6 Internet. Return packets follow the reverse path, using stored mapping information to route traffic back to the correct customer.

Critically, the ISP's legacy IPv4 network infrastructure remains largely unchanged. Existing IPv4-only customers can continue to access the IPv4 Internet as before. Customers with IPv6-capable equipment can obtain IPv6 connectivity. The system is transparent to the vast majority of the network.
sections.eli5: At home, a box handles old and new addresses. At the provider, a bigger box translates old addresses and unwraps tunneled new ones. The provider's main network sees mostly what it always did.

sections.title: How Packets Flow
sections.content:
An IPv4 packet from a customer's device travels to the home gateway, which either forwards it directly or applies address translation. The packet reaches the CGN, which applies a second layer of address translation (from customer-scope to public-scope), and forwards it to the IPv4 Internet. Return IPv4 packets follow the reverse path using NAT table entries.

An IPv6 packet from a customer's device reaches the home gateway, which encapsulates it in an IPv4 tunnel and sends it toward the CGN's IPv4 address. The CGN recognizes the tunnel, decapsulates the original IPv6 packet, and forwards it to the IPv6 Internet. When the customer receives IPv6 traffic from the Internet, the CGN re-encapsulates it in IPv4 and tunnels it back, and the home gateway removes the IPv4 wrapper before delivering the original IPv6 packet to the customer.

The document notes that while IPv4 traffic inherits all the limitations of CGN address sharing (limited support for inbound connections, difficulty with well-known ports), IPv6 traffic does not face these issues, creating an incentive for users and service providers to prefer IPv6 as the transition progresses.
sections.eli5: Old addresses bounce through two translators. New addresses get wrapped in old wrapping, unwrapped at the provider, and sent to the new network.

sections.title: Smooth Evolution
sections.content:
A key advantage of the incremental CGN approach is that the home gateway and CGN devices need not be replaced as the ISP's network evolves. Instead, their configuration and capabilities can change. In the simplest scenario, an ISP deploys incremental CGN devices running only IPv4 NAT initially. As plans develop, the ISP enables 6rd tunneling on the CGN and home gateways, allowing IPv6 connectivity without network changes.

Later, if the ISP decides to deploy native IPv6 routing throughout its network, the home gateway can detect native IPv6 Router Advertisement messages and stop using tunnels, switching to direct IPv6 forwarding. At that point, the CGN can drop its tunneling function and continue as a pure v4-v4 NAT device. Eventually, the ISP can transition to dual-stack routing throughout, or even IPv6-only operation, and the same physical devices can be reconfigured to support each phase.

This contrasts with the alternative approaches (pure CGN or 6rd alone), which do not support smooth transition. An ISP that has deployed pure CGN must later upgrade equipment to add IPv6 support. An ISP using only 6rd has not addressed the immediate IPv4 address shortage. Incremental CGN solves both problems with the same devices, allowing different regions of the ISP's network to be at different transition stages simultaneously.
sections.eli5: The boxes can change what they do just by reconfiguring. No rip-and-replace needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Limitations
sections.content:
The document acknowledges that incremental CGN introduces no fundamentally new security issues beyond those already present in NAT and CGN technology. Since the tunnels exist entirely within a single ISP's network between the customer and the CGN, the threat model is simple. However, operators should ensure that security mechanisms (such as packet inspection and firewall rules) are applied to IPv6 packets after decapsulation, and that the home gateway provides basic IPv6 security functionality.

The approach inherits all of CGN's IPv4 limitations: scaling difficulties, challenges supporting inbound connections on well-known ports, and application-layer problems caused by double NAT. Additionally, the use of IPv6 tunneling over IPv4 requires careful attention to MTU (maximum transmission unit) sizes to avoid excessive fragmentation. The document recommends an IPv6 tunnel MTU of at least 1500 bytes to preserve the user experience. IPv6 traffic, freed from NAT complications, will likely offer better performance and fewer headaches, creating natural incentives for applications to migrate.
sections.eli5: Security is similar to what providers already do. IPv4 has all the usual NAT problems. IPv6 works better, which helps push migration forward.
